notes: The previous note here said this DONE state exposes no Account, migration, takeover, shadow, or ML surface. Three of those five had become false and the sentence was never revisited: `ui/src/pages/MlRouting.tsx` is mounted as a routing tab and renders the gate's verdict, the shadow replay and a promotion round, and Providers renders a maintenance row per declared account. Corrected at the integration recorded in E-143; the status itself did not move, because the three gates this node owns — build, integration, smoke — were the same gates and still passed. **AND THE CORRECTION WAS ITSELF OUT OF DATE BEFORE IT WAS WRITTEN DOWN.** The clause that survived E-143 said "Migration and takeover still have no command and no surface", and by then both had: the takeover commands and page landed with the work this node records, and the migration engine now has four commands and a page of its own. A record that is corrected is corrected *once*; the sentence it replaced had already needed correcting twice, and each time it was the record that was late rather than the code that was wrong.

THE THREE OVERLAYS NOW BEHAVE ALIKE FOR THE KEYBOARD, AND TWO OF THEM DID NOT. The Drawer has always restored the focus to its opener on close, kept the focus inside itself and cycled Tab within itself. The confirm dialog focused its confirm button and then let the focus fall to the document body when it closed, so the next Tab started from the top of the page with nothing on screen saying that had happened. The popover claimed role="menu" with role="menuitem" children and implemented no arrow-key navigation at all, so a screen reader announced a menu and the arrow keys moved the page. A role is a promise about the behaviour and the arrow keys are the behaviour, so they are there now. Two new interaction cases cover it, and each was driven to failing before it was left passing. The gates live in scripts/ui_interaction_test.py, which is not a node of its own; this node records the behaviour rather than the harness.

THE DESKTOP SHELL NOW EXISTS, AND IT IS THE SAME PRODUCT AS THIS WINDOW. Four things a desktop application is expected to do that a web page cannot: be the only copy of itself, be summoned from another application, answer a zroutery:// URL, and say out loud when it failed with nobody looking at the window. A second launch used to carry on into the setup and fight the first one for the gateway port, because nothing saw it before the rest of the application started; the single-instance plugin is registered before every other plugin for that reason. The window is hidden by default, so the only way back to it was the menu bar, and a menu bar is not a shortcut: Ctrl+Shift+Alt+Z now summons it from any application, and a chord the operating system refuses is a warning rather than a reason to refuse to start. A zroutery:// link opens the page it names. And the gateway failing to start from the tray's start item — or at a silent login launch, where on macOS there is no window at all — is reported by a notification, because the tray menu has nowhere to write an error down; a failure that is already a banner in the dashboard is not repeated, since the same message twice is worse than one. The plugins are unconditional dependencies: the feature table is the product's own switchboard, and a desktop shell that changed shape with the ML stack would make the packaged binary depend on a learning flag. See E-148.

THE INTERFACE NOW SAYS ITS STATES IN WORDS, AND ITS CHINESE IN ITS OWN PUNCTUATION. A dot is a colour and a colour is invisible to a screen reader, and the dot is aria-hidden on purpose; every place the design used one to carry a fact had no way to say the fact. The activity timeline was the worst of them — the dot was the row's only sign of whether the request had worked. The word is a caller-supplied string rather than one chosen from the tone, because the tones have no single meaning: "ok" is a request that succeeded on the timeline and a model that is simply enabled on the models page. A field's hint is now a description rather than part of the control's name, and the DOM is deliberately unchanged: the tidier markup moved the hint out of the label, which changed the flex row the field is laid out in, and the layout harness refused it. The harness was right — a change that fixes an accessible name by moving a paragraph is a change that moves a paragraph. Ten toasts put the backend's English straight into a Chinese interface, and the Chinese table itself used ASCII commas and colons in 161 places, which read as though a translation machine had been through it. The English table is untouched, and the comments are left alone: they are read by developers, and the file's English comments use the ASCII marks. See E-149.

THE AUDIT'S REMAINING LIST, CORRECTED AND NOW THE ONLY ONE. A read-only pass over the whole interface found the items this work closed — the colour-only states, the toast that announced itself as "Dismiss", the field hint that was part of the control's name, the two overlays that fought each other, the menu that promised arrow keys and did not deliver them, the select that never said what it held, the select that never gave its placeholder back, the catalogue row that could not show its own "no tier" option, the dropdown inside a drawer that lost the focus to the drawer, the failed cutover that said nothing, the page with no heading on it, the English literals, the dead dictionary keys and the duplicated copy of the error boundary's strings, the dead card, the long id that made a row wider than the page, the controls that were named the same as every other one of their kind, the check-in that only spoke when it failed, the reports that were only visible, and the tabs and the menu that pointed at things that were not there — and a list of things it did not. What is still open is: a select's menu is portalled to the document body, which the focus guard now defers to, but which is still worth knowing about; the provider and model list rows still name themselves with an aria-label, which replaces the row's content in the accessibility tree, so the endpoint, the price and the latency are still not announced — the state was added to the name for exactly this reason, and the rest of the content is not in it; the takeover page matches the backend's reasons with English regular expressions, so a localised backend would stop matching; the type scale is fixed in pixels; and the strong border colour is 1.48:1 on white where a boundary that has to be seen wants 3:1 — which is left as it is on purpose, because reaching 3:1 means a visibly heavier grey that would undo a deliberately quiet monochrome design, and the elements it draws are decorations rather than the only thing that identifies a control. None of these is a blocker, and each is a decision rather than a slip — which is why they are written down instead of quietly left. An earlier revision of this note listed the items above as open; that list is gone rather than left beside this one, because two lists of what is open is one list too many and the older one is wrong.

THE DESKTOP SHELL HAS NOW BEEN DRIVEN, NOT ONLY COMPILED. Four plugins, a global shortcut and a URL scheme are the kind of thing that compiles and does not work: the shortcut is refused by the operating system, the scheme is not registered, a second launch starts a second gateway on a port the first one holds. The built executable was run and it said what it was doing. The shortcut was claimed. A second launch exited immediately with code 0 and wrote nothing, because it never reached the setup and so never started a second gateway, and the first instance survived. A link handed to the running instance as a second launch's argument arrived as "deep link opened: zroutery://providers" — the whole path, from a launch carrying a URL, through the single-instance handover, to the window that was already open. The one thing it said that could not have been true is also there: a debug build that was never installed has no scheme registered, and the shell says so rather than leaving a link that opens nothing unexplained. See E-157.

THE PANEL-BACKED BALANCE IS NOW PROVEN END TO END, AND IT WAS THE ONE BALANCE TEST THAT DID NOT EXIST. Every other balance test drove one piece — the sum of two quotas, the refusal to add two currencies, whether a provider has a balance to ask for at all — and none of them asked a panel. What a user gets when they press *查询余额* on a NewAPI relay is a longer chain: the provider's configuration, the account's own credential resolved through the secret store, an HTTP call to a panel the user cannot see from here, a quota parsed out of the answer and published into a store, read back out, summed, and rendered as a figure in dollars. Every link of that chain was proven on its own, and the chain itself was not proven at all. It is proven now, against a real panel on a real socket that answers the four endpoints the path reads and refuses everything else. **THE FIXTURE IS ARMED AGAINST THE THREE WAYS THIS TEST COULD PASS WHILE THE PRODUCT IS BROKEN**: the provider's own relay key is stored as well, so a path that resolved the provider's credential instead of the account's would meet a relay key where a dashboard token is required, and the adapter refuses to be built with one; the panel records the credentials it was given; and it refuses any credential it was not told to accept. **WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE IS THE REASON THE `NEWAPI` NODE IS STILL PARTIAL**, which is that no *real* panel has ever answered this adapter. A panel on loopback that answers what it is told is still a panel this test wrote. See E-160.

THE PAGES HAVE NOW BEEN READ IN A REAL BROWSER, AND ONE OF THEM HAD NEVER BEEN LOOKED AT. The cutover page, the provider drawer and the accounts page were rendered against the built interface and read out of the page: the OpenCode provider kinds are offered where the build can serve them; the balance chip carries the figure the panel reported and the button that asks the panel is enabled; the drawer's account section explains in the operator's own language that a relay key (`sk-…`) cannot authenticate a panel and the panel's access token belongs there instead; and the accounts page shows a declared account as unprobed with its credential not yet stored, rather than as an empty list. The cutover page shows the plan for the client, each step marked as undoable or not, and its confirmation states that the file is captured byte for byte before anything is written — and that the undo applies only to a failed run. **AND THE READING FOUND A FAULT IN THE TOOL, NOT IN THE PRODUCT.** The preview answered every command with the snapshot, so the page that asked for a list of plans was handed an object and said so in a minified variable name. The real command returns a list; the fault was the stub answering with the wrong shape. **WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE IS THE STATEMENT THAT IS STILL TRUE**: the cutover page has not been driven in the *running application* by a person, and a browser against a stubbed backend is not that. The check-in row remains the one surface here that has been. See E-160 and E-161.

THE AUTO MODE CAN NOW BE JUDGED BY A DECISION MODEL, AND THE DASHBOARD SAYS SO. The Auto Mode asked a language model a binary question — may this action proceed? — and read the answer out of a `<block>yes</block>` tag. A decision model answers the same question in its own protocol: a state, a typed question, and a calibrated probability instead of prose. So the proxy is the one that has to speak both. It asks the decision endpoint in the decision protocol and **speaks the answer back in the client's own protocol** — the client receives `<block>yes</block>` or `<block>no</block>`, exactly what a language model's verdict would have looked like, and nothing downstream knows which kind of model answered. **A PROBABILITY IS NOT A VERDICT, AND THE THRESHOLD IS WHERE THE TWO MEET.** The Auto Mode is a security gate, so an answer that is not confident has not cleared the action and the action is blocked — the same rule the text verdict already followed, where an unreadable answer is not an allow. The threshold is the confidence the answer must carry in either direction; the default is the detector's own floor, and 0.5 lets a calibrated model's own majority decide. **THE DASHBOARD OFFERS IT AS WHAT IT IS.** A decision provider is a fifth provider kind, with its own section in the provider drawer — the path its endpoint answers on, and the confidence the answer must carry — and a relay carries neither, because neither means anything for a relay. The Auto Mode pool can hold a decision model by name, and the model is declared by hand on the models page, because a decision endpoint publishes no catalogue. **AND A DECISION MODEL IS NOT OFFERED FOR MAIN TRAFFIC.** It answers typed questions and cannot answer a request that wants prose, so it is not a tier member, it is not published in the model listing, and it is not a candidate for the tier pools. **A NOTE ABOUT WHERE THIS SITS**: the Auto Mode's classifier has no node of its own — the record of it is the history treatment map's T02 — so the evidence is the record here, and the gate is `crates/zroutery-core/tests/decision_model_test.rs` with the dashboard's half in the interaction suite. See E-164.

THE DASHBOARD DOES NOT OFFER A DECISION MODEL A TIER, AND SAYS WHY INSTEAD. Adding the capability put two more controls on screen that the build cannot honour, and they were the same defect this project has been fixing all along. A decision model answers the Auto Mode's questions and cannot answer a request that wants prose, so the router excludes it from every tier pool — which means a tier the dashboard let the operator pick would be one the router silently ignored. And a decision endpoint publishes no catalogue, so the *fetch catalogue* button would have asked it for a model list it does not have. **So both are gone, and the reason is where the control was.** The tier control is disabled rather than hidden: a hidden control leaves the row looking like an oversight, and a disabled one that does not say why is a control that refuses for no visible reason. The catalogue button is replaced by a sentence saying where the model is declared instead — by hand, on the models page. **AND THE DRAWER OF A RELAY CARRIES NEITHER**, which is what makes it a rule rather than a special case. **THE READING FOUND A DUPLICATED LABEL THAT THE WRITE-UP MISSED**: the explanation's own row was labelled *Tier*, so the drawer showed two rows called Tier, the second being the sentence explaining the first. It is now *Why no tier* / *为何没有层级*. See E-166.

THE AUTO MODE'S EDITOR NOW SAYS HOW A VERDICT ARRIVES, AND NAMES BOTH WAYS. It told the operator that a verdict is parsed *only* from `<block>yes|no</block>`, and that was true while every candidate answered in prose — and it stopped being true when a decision model could answer with a probability instead. So the sentence the operator reads was wrong about the thing it describes, which is the kind of sentence that costs an hour of debugging at the wrong end. The row now names the tag a language model answers with and the probability a decision model answers with, and names the threshold on the provider as what decides which of them counts as a verdict. **THE SAME KIND OF SENTENCE WAS FOUND IN TWO PLACES AND FIXED IN TWO PLACES**: the provider's drawer had a tier control that refused for no visible reason, and the models page's drawer had one that refused with the reason beside it. Both drawers now carry it, because both are drawers the operator is in when they set the thing up.

THE PROVIDER DRAWER'S ENDPOINT ROW NOW SAYS THE URL THE DECISION REQUEST USES, NOT THE HALF IT STARTS FROM. A relay's base url is its endpoint, so the row showed the base for every provider; a decision endpoint's address is the base plus the path it answers on, and the row was showing a string the request never uses. The join is not the obvious one — `/v1` is inserted unless the path already begins with it — so `/systemone` and `/v1/systemone` name the same endpoint, and an operator checking the address can now see which one they typed. **THE MIRROR IS DOCUMENTED** (`DecisionConfig::url`), the Rust side keeps the authority, and the end-to-end decision test exercises the identity branch against a real socket. **THE BROWSER CHECK USED `/systemone` ON PURPOSE**, so the displayed `https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` proved the inserted `/v1` rather than echoing back the path that was typed. See E-168.

THE AUTO MODE'S POOL LET A DECISION MODEL IN BY NAME AND THEN SHOWED IT EXACTLY LIKE A CHAT MODEL. The pool takes a model id, not a provider, so the one candidate that is asked a typed question and answers with a probability looked like the ones asked for prose and answering with a tag — the same defect as the editor's sentence, one level earlier. The add menu now says `jev-jev · Decision model` and the row carries the same badge, before and after the choice, with the sentence explaining the probability a few lines below them. **READING THE ROW FOUND THE LAST HARD-CODED ENGLISH LABEL IN THE DASHBOARD**: the pool's enable box was `aria-label="Enable jev-jev"` on the Chinese page, so a Chinese screen reader switched language mid-sentence; it is now `启用 jev-jev`. **THAT HALF IS OBSERVED RATHER THAN GATED**: the interaction suite pins English, which cannot tell the new label from the old one, so the Chinese label was read in the browser. The badge and the menu label are gated by UI-21, which adds the decision model through the real menu and reads both. See E-169.
